title: Garbure
subtitle: A thick Gascon broth of cabbage, beans, and preserved pork
excerpt: A dense, slow-simmered soup from Gascony packed with savoy cabbage, butter beans, potato, and ham hock. It is closer to a stew than a soup and eats as a full meal.
sourceNotes: Traditional Gascon peasant dish from south-west France. Classically made with confit duck or salt pork; ham hock gives similar depth.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions without the bread. Reheat gently on the hob and add fresh bread to serve.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. The flavour improves the next day.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a day ahead. The soup thickens overnight; add a little water when reheating.

content.text: Garbure is a Gascon workhorse: a thick, filling soup built from whatever is in the garden and the curing shed. The ham hock gives it deep, smoky body. Let it simmer slowly so the cabbage softens completely and the broth turns rich.

items.prepNote: white and pale green parts, sliced

content.text: Put the ham hock in the dutch oven. Cover with the water. Bring to a boil and skim off any grey foam.
Add the onion, garlic, leek, carrot, thyme, and bay leaves. Reduce to a steady simmer.
Simmer for 60 minutes until the hock is tender. Lift it out and leave to cool slightly.
Add the potato to the broth. Cook for 10 minutes.
Add the cabbage and butter beans. Cook for 15 more minutes until the cabbage is fully tender.
Pull the meat from the hock and tear into chunks. Discard the skin and bone. Stir the meat back into the pot.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Ladle over slices of toasted bread in deep bowls.

items.symptom: The broth is thin and watery.
items.fix: Ladle out a cup of the potato and beans, mash them, and stir back in to thicken the broth.

items.symptom: The ham is salty but the vegetables taste flat.
items.cause: The hock was heavily cured and the salt spread unevenly.
items.fix: Soak the hock in cold water for 2 hours before cooking. Taste the broth before adding any salt.

items.symptom: The cabbage is still tough after cooking.
items.cause: It went in too late or the simmer dropped too low.
items.fix: Add the cabbage earlier, at the same time as the potato, and keep a steady simmer throughout.
